newsitem.title: USA: Ford sees Mazda cost-savings starting in '98.
newsitem.headline: Ford sees Mazda cost-savings starting in '98.

text.p: Ford Motor Co, after a year coordinating product development plans with Mazda Motor Corp, said Thursday it expects the partnership to start yielding real cost savings next year.

Ford Vice Chairman Wayne Booker declined to put a dollar amount on the realized or potential savings that will fall to the U.S. No. 2 automaker's bottom line from its Mazda ventures, other than to say it will be "substantial."

Booker spoke to reporters at Ford's Dearborn headquarters to mark the one-year anniversary of Ford increasing its stake in the Japanese automaker to 33.4 percent. A similar meeting was held in Japan with Mazda President Henry Wallace.

"This past year has been primarily one of organization, one of sorting out cycle plan priorities, and therefore we haven't seen material savings to date," said Booker, who oversees the automaker's international operations.
"We've seen some savings, enough to know that it works," he said.

Booker said the two companies have cemented future plans that call for Mazda to differentiate its vehicles through styling and performance, while borrowing more heavily from Ford components than it has in the past.

Many of the new joint product plans, finalized last month, will show up in commercial vehicles for Asian markets, he said. As part of its Asian growth plans, Ford hopes to take advantage of one of Mazda's core strengths: light commercial vehicles that are well-suited for delivering goods in small, narrow streets.

Also in Asia, Ford plans to launch other product and manufacturing ventures with Mazda. Booker would not disclose details, but said the developments would be smaller in scope than the Auto Alliance (Thailand) Co Ltd the two firms own.
That company will launch a new compact pickup truck this fall and eventually be capable of producing more than 100,000 units annually.

The two automakers settled on at least one more all new joint product for the North American market, said Booker, declining to elaborate. Analysts said Ford is collaborating with Mazda on a new, subcompact sport/utility vehicle.

When the current Escort small car progam is through, Ford and Mazda will not have a passenger car project in North America, although Booker said there will be cooperative car efforts in other parts of the world.
No changes are planned for the comapny's compact pickup truck arrangement. Mazda currently sells a version of the Ford Ranger as its B-Series pickup truck.

Ford's ties to Mazda date back to 1969, when the two agreed to jointly make automatic transmissions in Japan. Mazda, Japan's fifth-largest automaker, has historically been known for its high quality small displacement engines and manual transmissions, but has struggled in recent years with losses and falling marketshare.
